title: PL/0
help_lit: Pushes value to the top of the stack.
help_int: Increases or decreases the stack pointer. Increasing beyond already generated stack creates 0s. Cannot decrease stack pointer under the current stack frame or under -1.
help_opr: Performs operation (logic or arithmetic). The instruction behaves just like the reference interpreter (operations 1 - 13). If the operation uses two values from stack, the first value is the one with the lower index and the second value is the one on top of the stack. Division (5) is an integer division rounded towards zero and the result of modulo (6) has the sign of the dividend. Unlike Wirth's original PL/0, where operation 6 is 'odd' and there is no modulo, operation 6 is modulo and 7 is 'odd'.
help_opr2:
Available operations:
1 - Unary minus
2 - Addition
3 - Subtraction
4 - Multiplication
5 - Division
6 - Modulo
7 - Is odd
8 - Equal
9 - Not equal
10 - Less than
11 - More or equal than
12 - More than
13 - Less or equal than
help_jmp: Jumps to the instruction specified by address. If the jump would end up on a non-existent instruction, an exception is thrown.
help_jmc: If there is 0 on the top of the stack, jumps to the instruction specified by the address. The value is removed from the stack in both cases. If the jump would end up on a non-existent instruction, an exception is thrown. The name JPC from Wirth's original PL/0 is accepted as well.
help_lod: Loads a value from level, address on the stack and pushes it into the stack. If the level is too high (the target stack frame would end up under the first stack frame) an exception is thrown.
help_sto: Stores the value on top of the stack to level, address on stack. If the level is too high (the target stack frame would end up under the first stack frame) an exception is thrown.
help_cal: Creates a new stack frame with static base (SB) at relative index 0, dynamic base (DB) at relative index 1 and program counter (PC) at relative index 2.
help_cal2: The static base is set levels down, so when the level is 0, the static base is set as the caller's current base, and when the level is 1 the static base is set as the current caller's static base. Otherwise, the static base is resolved by iterating over the static bases of the stack frames under the caller.
help_cal3: The dynamic base is set as the caller's current base. The program counter is set as the next instruction to be executed (PC + 1).
help_cal4: Then a jump is done to the instruction specified by address. The stack pointer has to be increased through the INT instruction (same as the reference interpreter).
help_ret: Sets the program counter (PC) to the value stored on the stack frame's index 2. Sets the stack pointer to current base - 1 (the top of previous stack frame). Sets the current base to the dynamic base (DB) stored on the stack frame's index 1. The return instruction OPR 0 0 of Wirth's original PL/0 is accepted as RET.
help_ret2: If the instruction is executed while the current base is 0 (aka the first stack frame), the program exits.
help_rea: Reads one character from the input field, converts it to a number and pushes it into the stack. The character is expected to be ASCII (or Extended ASCII, simply an 8-bit value). If there is no character in the input field or the character is not an Extended ASCII character (its code is above 255), an exception is thrown.
help_wri: Writes the value from the top of the stack into the output field as a character. If the value is not in range <0, 255>, an exception is thrown.
help_new: Takes the value on top of the stack as the number of heap cells to allocate. Allocates that many cells continuously (in one continuous block) and pushes the address of the block onto the stack. If the cells cannot be allocated, -1 is pushed onto the stack (e.g. not enough free cells, invalid value).
help_del: Takes the value on top of the stack as the address of the heap block to deallocate. The heap block is deallocated in its entirety. On failure throws an exception.
help_lda: Takes the value on top of the stack as the address of the heap cell. Pushes the value in the heap cell onto the stack. Throws an exception on failure.
help_sta: Takes the value on top of the stack as the value to store and the value under it (SP - 1) as the address to store it at. Stores the value at the address in heap. On failure throws an exception.
help_pld: Essentially a dynamic LOD, where the address is the value on top of the stack and the level is the value under it (SP - 1). Pushes the value from specified address and level of the stack onto the stack.
help_pst: Essentially a dynamic STO, where the address is the value on top of the stack, the level is the value under it (SP - 1) and the value to be stored is on the index SP - 2. Stores the specified value into the specified address and level of the stack.
help_itr: Takes two values from the top of the stack and understands them as two parts of decimal number. The number under the top of the stack (SP - 1) is the integer part and the number on top of the stack is the fractional part. Pushes mantissa and exponent in the base of 10 onto the stack (mantissa * 10^exponent). Mantissa will be on top of the stack and exponent under it.
help_rti: Takes two values from the top of the stack and understands them as mantissa and exponent in the base of 10. The number on top of the stack is the mantissa and the number under the top of the stack (SP - 1) is the exponent. Pushes two integers onto the stack, which can be understood as the integer and fractional part of the decimal number. Fractional part will be on top of the stack and integer part under it.
help_rti2: Parameter can either be 0 or 1. If it is 1, the number will be stripped of its fractional part and the integer part will be the only part pushed to the stack. With parameter set to 0 this instruction works as said above.
help_opf: Performs operation (logic or arithmetic). The instruction behaves just like the reference interpreter (operations 1 - 13). The only difference between OPR and OPF is that OPF uses floating points, so binary operations take four values from the stack (two for each operand - mantissa and exponent) and unary operations (1 and 7) take two. Results are truncated to 6 significant digits.

help_lit_halt: Does not halt system under normal execution.
help_int_halt: Halts system if attempting to decrease SP below current stack frame base or below -1.
help_opr_halt: Halts system on division or modulo by zero (operations 5 and 6), or if there are fewer operands on stack than required.
help_jmp_halt: Halts system if target address is negative (< 0) or points to non-existent memory.
help_jmc_halt: Halts system if stack is empty, or if condition is met and target address is negative or points to non-existent memory.
help_lod_halt: Halts system if static link level difference is too high (under root frame) or the resulting stack index is negative. Note: a negative address (e.g. LOD 0 -1 reads a value pushed by the caller below the frame base) and reading unallocated memory log a soft warning without halting.
help_sto_halt: Halts system if stack is empty, level difference is too high or the resulting stack index is negative. Note: a negative address (writing below the frame base), overwriting frame control links or unallocated memory log soft warnings without halting.
help_cal_halt: Halts system if level difference is too high or procedure address is negative or out of bounds.
help_ret_halt: Terminates normally when returning from base frame (base 0). Halts system with error if return PC was corrupted to negative or out-of-bounds address.
help_rea_halt: Halts system if input text stream is empty (no characters available) or the next character is not in range <0, 255>.
help_wri_halt: Halts system if stack is empty or ASCII value is out of range <0, 255>.
help_new_halt: Does not halt system on allocation failure (pushes -1 with a soft warning). Halts if stack is empty.
help_del_halt: Halts system if stack is empty, or if attempting to free an unallocated block, metadata, or an already freed block (double-free). A negative address wraps around to the end of the heap (-1 is the last cell) and logs a warning.
help_lda_halt: Halts system if stack is empty or heap address is out of bounds (>= heap size or < -heap size). A negative address wraps around to the end of the heap (-1 is the last cell) and logs a warning without halting, like reading metadata or an unallocated cell.
help_sta_halt: Halts system if stack has fewer than 2 operands or heap address is out of bounds (>= heap size or < -heap size). A negative address wraps around to the end of the heap (-1 is the last cell) and logs a warning without halting, like overwriting metadata or an unallocated cell.
help_pld_halt: Halts system if stack has fewer than 2 operands, the level is invalid or too high, or the resulting stack index is negative. A negative address (below the frame base) logs a soft warning without halting.
help_pst_halt: Halts system if stack has fewer than 3 operands, the level is invalid or too high, or the resulting stack index is negative. A negative address (below the frame base) and overwriting frame links log a soft warning without halting.
help_itr_halt: Halts system if stack has fewer than 2 operands.
help_rti_halt: Halts system if stack has fewer than 2 operands.
help_opf_halt: Halts system if stack has insufficient operands. Note: Floating-point division and modulo by zero do NOT halt system (they produce Infinity, -Infinity, or NaN with a soft warning, unlike integer OPR).

cliHelpTitle: Headless Command Line Interface & Debug Directives
cliHelpDesc: PL/0 programs can be executed headlessly from the command line for automated testing, batch grading, and compiler verification.
cliHelpDirectivesNote: Directives can be placed on a standalone line (e.g. &REGS) or inside comments (; &REGS, // &STK). They execute during standard runs and print their output directly to the standard output area (and standard output in CLI) without altering calculation state or bytecode instruction indices.
helpDirectivesExampleComment: Stores 5 into a variable and inspects it with directives
directive_regs: Prints register contents: Base register (BASE), Stack Pointer (SP), Program Counter (PC), and caller frame links.
directive_stk: Prints entire stack contents from index 0 to top of stack (SP) with special slot markers.
directive_stka: Prints stack contents starting from the base register, representing the active activation record (current frame).
directive_stkn: Prints the last n items from the top of stack.
directive_stkrg: Prints stack contents from memory address a to address b inclusive.
directive_echo: Prints arbitrary text message to the debug output stream.
directive_mem: Prints memory footprint summary (stack depth, heap data cells, active blocks, and peak total memory).
directive_heap: Prints detailed status of allocated blocks and memory addresses on the dynamic heap.
directive_assert_tos: Asserts that the top of stack equals expected value without popping it.
directive_stats: Prints a snapshot of instruction execution and profiling statistics.
dragToResize: Drag to resize memory and statistics
